author: Vitor
notes: Too slow for actual acceptance, TLE was expected. 668 / 682 testcases passed.
aiExplanation: This solution first **sorts indices by their values** and assigns each one to a connectivity `group` (a new group starts whenever consecutive sorted values differ by more than `maxDiff`, mirroring day 9's grouping trick). Within each group it then builds a full `n x n` **memoized distance table** `dp`, walking backward from each sorted position and greedily counting how many `maxDiff` "hops" are needed to connect back to earlier indices in the same group, storing that hop count only in `dp[arr[i]][arr[j]]` (not the symmetric `dp[arr[j]][arr[i]]`). It times out mainly because allocating and filling an `n x n` table is `O(n^2)` in both time and memory, which is far too slow for large `n`.

author: Vitor
notes: Test to check difference of using Math.max on every query. No difference at all, same TLE as before.
aiExplanation: Nearly identical to the previous attempt — it sorts indices by value, buckets them into connectivity `groups`, and fills an `n x n` `dp` table with the minimum number of `maxDiff` hops between pairs — except this time it also writes the **symmetric entry** `dp[arr[j]][arr[i]] = dist`, so lookups no longer need `Math.max(dp[u][v], dp[v][u])`. It still times out for the same reason as before: building and storing an `O(n^2)` table is too slow and memory-heavy for large inputs.

author: Vitor + Claude
notes: Used Claude (free account) to figure out how my solution could be improved. Binary lifting (whatever that is) was the answer, and the results were seriously impressive: 100 / 100.
aiExplanation: This accepted solution uses **binary lifting** to answer each query in logarithmic time instead of building a full distance table. It first sorts indices into rank order and assigns a `group` id to each contiguous run of values within `maxDiff` of their neighbor (same connectivity trick as before). Then, using a two-pointer sweep, it computes `next0[k]`: the farthest rank reachable in **one greedy hop** from rank `k` (the widest possible single step still within `maxDiff`). From that base, it builds an `up` table where `up[j][k]` stores the rank reached after `2^j` hops from `k`, doubling the jump size at each level — a classic sparse-table/binary-lifting structure. For each query, if the two indices aren't in the same `group` the answer is `-1`; otherwise `minHops` walks the `up` table from the largest power of two down to zero, greedily taking any jump that doesn't overshoot the target, to compute the **minimum number of hops** in `O(log n)`, making the whole algorithm `O(n log n)` overall instead of `O(n^2)`.
